neighbours.label: the key noun of a named social or policy concept at the point an argumentative passage singles it out as the thing at issue ('the tyranny of the [majority]', 'total ab[stinence]', 'code of [honor]', 'the "[CSI] effect"'); not the same nouns in neutral, concrete use
fire: The deepest flaw of popular government, he wrote, is the tyranny of the majority, which crushes dissent more surely than any king.
Some clinicians hold that controlled drinking is a myth, and that the only safe goal for an alcoholic is lifelong abstinence. Others doubt it.
Duels were defended not by law but by an appeal to the old and bloody code of honor. Even judges bowed to it.
Carbohydrates, not butter, drive weight gain, whatever the old advice said. The low fat diet has left many people hungrier.
Prosecutors complain that jurors now expect forensic proof in every trial. They call this the "CSI effect" and argue about whether it is real.
Insurers know there is one group that takes the wildest risks behind the wheel, and it is teenage males, the daredevils of every town.
The worst vice of a free press, critics say, is the cult of celebrity, which pushes out real news.
The great weakness of central planning, he argued, was the knowledge problem, since no office can know what millions want.
quiet: The majority of the students arrived early and sat near the front of the hall, waiting for the lecture to begin.
The clinic opens at nine, and the nurses see about forty patients before lunch. Others come later.
The old school gave an honor roll certificate to every pupil who finished the year. Even parents got one.
Butter, flour and sugar go into the bowl first. The fat should be cold when you rub it in.
The lab processes forensic samples for the county police. They call the courier at noon and send the results by post.
The farm keeps one group of calves in the lower barn, and it is the males, which are sold in spring.
The local paper prints a weekly column about gardening, which runs next to the crossword.
The office kept a list of every order, he said, since the customers often phoned to ask about them.

notes: Card: ' majority' x2, 'stinence', ' honor', ' fat', 'CSI', ' males', all in opinionated commentary. One-line probes were weak (<= 0.17), but two-clause argumentative passages fired: 'tyranny of the majority' 0.59, 'total abstinence' 0.62, 'low fat diet' 0.32; 'the majority of the apples' 0.03, 'young males' 0.03. Needs argumentative context; the - pole is flagged broad.
